opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, we've spent the last decade getting very good at training neural networks, and as a community we've produced an enormous number of them: model zoos, checkpoints on Hugging Face, all the intermediate snapshots saved during training runs. Usually we treat these as end products. You train a model, you evaluate it, you deploy it, and the weights themselves are kind of a black box we don't look at much.

The central idea for us is to flip that around and say: what if the trained weights themselves are a data modality? Just like we learn representations of images or text, can we learn representations of neural networks by looking at large populations of them? We sometimes call these "hyper-representations." The model zoo becomes the dataset, and each network is one sample.

The goals are a couple of things. One is analysis. If you have a good representation of a network's weights, can you predict properties of that model without running it on data? Things like its test accuracy, its generalization gap, which hyperparameters it was trained with, or which stage of training it's in. That turns out to work surprisingly well, which tells you the weights carry a lot of structured information.

The second goal, which I find even more exciting, is generation. If you've learned a meaningful latent space over model weights, you can sample from it and produce new weights, for example to initialize models, do transfer learning, or build ensembles, without going through the full training procedure each time.

There are real challenges. Neural networks have symmetries, for instance you can permute neurons in a layer and get exactly the same function with different weights. So the representation learning has to respect or exploit those symmetries, and we use things like data augmentation through permutations and contrastive or reconstruction-based objectives. Scaling to large models is another open problem, since you can't just flatten billions of parameters into a vector.

Underneath all of it is the more fundamental question: is there a learnable structure to the space of trained neural networks? Our results so far suggest there is, and that makes populations of models a really rich resource we've mostly been ignoring.

r001.rationale: It explicitly presents predicting model properties, including accuracy and generalization gap, as a goal of learning representations from populations of networks.

r002.rationale: It describes generating new weights for initialization, transfer learning, or ensembles, but does not frame modifying a network’s behavior as a goal.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. The way I think about it is this: we have, at this point, millions of trained neural networks sitting in public repositories. Hugging Face, model zoos, all of it. And each of those models is the result of a very expensive process. Someone collected data, designed an architecture, ran an optimizer for days or weeks, and what came out is a set of weights. That set of weights encodes everything the model learned. But today we basically treat those weights as a black box. We download them, we run inference, maybe we fine-tune, and that's it.

So the central question for us is: can we treat the trained weights themselves as a data modality? Not the images the model was trained on, not the text, but the parameters. Can we learn representations of those, the same way we learn representations of images or sentences?

The motivation is that the weight space carries a lot of information. If I give you a population of models, say a few thousand small CNNs trained on different datasets with different hyperparameters, the weights encode which dataset it saw, how far it got in training, whether it generalizes well, whether it's robust to adversarial inputs, and so on. Our goal is to learn an embedding, a hyper-representation as we call it, where you can read off those properties without having to run the model on a test set. You just look at the weights and you can predict accuracy, predict the training data, predict hyperparameters.

And then the second half, which I find even more exciting, is the generative direction. Once you have a good representation of weight space, you can sample from it. You can generate new models. You can take an embedding, decode it, and get a set of weights that already works reasonably well as an initialization, or that transfers to a new task. So instead of training from scratch every time, you draw from a learned distribution over models.

The hard part, and this is where a lot of our work sits, is that weight space has a lot of structure and a lot of symmetries. You can permute neurons in a layer and get a functionally identical network with completely different weight vectors. So a naive approach that just flattens the weights and feeds them into an encoder tends to learn the wrong thing. We spend a lot of effort on tokenization of weights, on augmentations that respect those symmetries, and on self-supervised objectives that make the representation capture function rather than the particular arrangement of parameters.

But the big picture goal is really that simple to state: neural networks are now artifacts we produce at scale, and we should be learning from the collection of them, not just from each one in isolation.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly states that learned weight representations should predict properties such as accuracy, training data, and hyperparameters across a population of models.

r002.rationale: The response describes generating new models and using them as initializations or for transfer, but does not frame modifying neural network behavior as a goal.

astra-6.text:
The central idea is to treat trained neural networks themselves as data. Normally, we learn a representation of an image or a piece of text. Here, we ask: can we learn a representation of a model from its weights, using a collection of trained models as our dataset?

What makes that interesting is that each network contains information about the data it has seen and the process through which it learned. We want a representation that captures meaningful differences in what those networks have learned, while ignoring differences that are simply due to how the parameters are arranged. Two networks can implement the same function even though their weights look quite different.

If we can do that, we can reason about models in a shared representation space: compare them, predict their properties, and ultimately use the knowledge in that collection to help build new models. So the goal is to make the experience accumulated across trained networks reusable.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly lists predicting model properties as a goal of reasoning from a shared representation of trained networks.

r002.rationale: The response says the collected knowledge could help build new models, but does not clearly state that modifying neural network behavior is a goal.

sol-6.1.text:
The central idea is to treat trained neural networks themselves as data. Each network is an artifact of a learning process: its parameters encode something about the data it saw, the task it was trained on, and the optimization that produced it. If we have a collection of these networks, can we learn a representation that captures what they have in common and how they differ?

The goal is a space where distance is meaningful in terms of the networks’ behavior or capabilities. Simply comparing weights is difficult, because two networks can implement the same function with very different parameter configurations. So we want to capture the underlying structure that matters. That could let us characterize a network, predict properties of it, or eventually use what we’ve learned across many networks to help construct new ones.

r001.rationale: It explicitly says the learned representation could be used to predict properties of a network.

r002.rationale: It mentions using what is learned to help construct new networks, but does not frame modifying a network’s behavior as a goal.
